extracted.intended_audience: electric cooperative leaders, policymakers, federal agencies (EPA/DOE/FERC), and other stakeholders in U.S. grid reliability and permitting policy
extracted.subtask_short: advocacy comments on EPA power rule
extracted.subtask_description: Materials and guidance for preparing advocacy/notice-and-comment responses and legislative outreach about EPA power-plant regulation, permitting reform, and grid reliability from the perspective of electric cooperatives. Focuses on policy/design criteria, procedural timelines, and priorities co-ops want regulators and Congress to adopt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural gas plant BSER and compliance timelines
rubrics_metrics.description: Existing natural gas plants of at least 300 megawatts and a capacity factor above 50% are expected to install 90% effective CCS by 2035 or co-fire with 30% low-carbon hydrogen beginning in 2032 and almost entirely hydrogen by 2038. New natural gas plants providing baseload must meet the same CCS or hydrogen standards as large existing natural gas plants. Plants used intermittently must co-fire with 30% low-carbon hydrogen by 2032, while peaking units must meet low-emitting fuels requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are prescriptive technology/timeline requirements in EPA's proposed rule; advocacy can evaluate feasibility, reliability impacts, permitting implications, supply chain and fuel-availability constraints, and the likely retirement decisions they would prompt. Use the specified MW, capacity-factor, percent-CCS, hydrogen co-fire percentages and the 2032/2035/2038 milestone years when commenting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coal unit BSER dependent on retirement date
rubrics_metrics.description: The Best System of Emission Reduction (BSER) for coal units retiring before 2040 will depend on their shutdown date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This ties emissions-control expectations to retirement timing; comments should examine how the BSER is applied across different retirement horizons and the resulting operational and reliability consequences. Consider whether the rule’s treatment of near-term retirements is realistic given replacement capacity timelines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize five top issues affecting reliable electricity delivery
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA must acknowledge five top issues affecting reliable delivery: increasing demand for electricity as more sectors electrify; decreasing electricity supply due to disorderly retirement and insufficient replacement of existing generation; permitting delays preventing new generation and transmission; supply chain challenges; and challenges with natural gas availability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this five-point list as an evaluative checklist when assessing rule impacts: quantify demand growth, forecast retirements and replacement capacity, identify permitting bottlenecks, analyze supply-chain lead times for critical equipment, and assess natural gas availability risks. Demonstrate how a rule would interact with or exacerbate these five issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative procedural timeline for commenting and hearings
rubrics_metrics.description: NRECA notes the EPA's public comment phase will open 60 days after publication in the Federal Register, and EPA will hold a virtual public hearing at a date to be determined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For preparing notice-and-comment submissions and stakeholder engagement, track the 60-day comment window and plan participation in any virtual hearing. Timely filings and registration for hearings are necessary to ensure input is considered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time limits for environmental reviews (NEPA) — two-year maximum
rubrics_metrics.description: Establish time limits of no more than two years for environmental reviews. 'That should be enough time to conduct a rigorous review while providing project certainty.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a specific legislative/policy recommendation for NEPA reform: proposals should include concrete statutory/regulatory deadlines (≤2 years) and mechanisms to meet them. When advocating, provide evidence (e.g., average EIS times ~4.5 years, quartile >6 years) and suggest how agencies could meet the 2-year target without sacrificing rigor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Greater applicant involvement in the permitting process
rubrics_metrics.description: Permit applicants (e.g., member-owned co-ops) should have greater involvement in the process because they 'know the specific details of their projects and the unique needs and challenges facing their communities.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comments can request statutory or procedural changes to increase applicant input (e.g., early coordination, structured applicant-contributed data, joint scoping). However, maintain a clear statement that federal agencies should retain final decision authority while improving applicant engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expedited, proportionate reviews for recurring small projects
rubrics_metrics.description: More efficient reviews are needed for recurring small projects—such as trimming trees to prevent power outages and wildfires—that are known to have minimal environmental impacts. 'Electric co-ops should not have to navigate a lengthy, bureaucratic process for actions where both co-ops and the agency already know the benefits are high and the impacts are low.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advocate for categorical exclusions, programmatic NEPA documents, or shortened review tracks for repetitive low-impact activities. Provide examples and data on environmental impacts to justify eligibility for streamlined treatment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit lengthy, costly litigation and set time limits on lawsuits
rubrics_metrics.description: Limit lengthy, costly litigation that can delay projects indefinitely. 'Litigation can result in excessive paperwork and unnecessary delays—holding up projects that communities badly need.' Recommendation to put time limits on how long someone can wait before filing a lawsuit after an agency grants a permit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposals may include statutory limitations on post-decision suit windows, expedited judicial review timelines, or procedural bars to repetitious litigation. When commenting, cite cases and timelines showing project delays from litigation and propose balanced safeguards for public participation and environmental law enforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure transmission permitting and siting improvements reflect co-op and community needs
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure that transmission permitting and siting improvements reflect co-op and community needs. 'The electric grid needs more electric grid transmission capacity to meet expected growth in the coming decades.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advocate for stakeholder input mechanisms, local-benefit analyses, cost-allocation rules that align costs with tangible beneficiaries, and siting processes that consider rural/community priorities. Provide specific examples where current siting/permitting processes have failed local needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allocate costs only to those who receive tangible and quantifiable benefits
rubrics_metrics.description: Policies to spur additional capacity must allocate the costs only to those who receive tangible and quantifiable benefits and 'must ultimately serve the national interest of maintaining the reliability and affordability of the electric grid.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comments can push for cost-allocation principles in transmission and other projects that prevent cross-subsidization by customers who do not benefit. Supply methodologies or precedent for beneficiary-pays cost allocation to show feasibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduce administrative paperwork burden for RUS/USDA funding applications
rubrics_metrics.description: RUS is shrinking the size of environmental review paperwork required for loans from a minimum of 70 pages down to just four pages to expedite co-op construction projects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage regulators/agencies to adopt similar paperwork reductions and streamlined forms for clearly eligible projects. When proposing process changes, show how shorter forms can preserve environmental safeguards while reducing delay and cost.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid rapid retirement of dispatchable generation without adequate replacement
rubrics_metrics.description: Retiring dispatchable generating resources (coal and gas) at a pace and in an amount that is too fast threatens the ability to keep the lights on; policymakers must consider near-term reliability before implementing standards that could exacerbate shortages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyses submitted in comments should model capacity adequacy, dispatchable reserve margins, and timing of replacements. Advocate for transition timelines and reliability backstops (e.g., capacity markets, reliability contracts, staged retirements) to avoid supply shortfalls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for supply-chain constraints and lead times
rubrics_metrics.description: Supply chain challenges (e.g., two-year lead times for critical transformers; previously six-to-13 months pre-COVID) constrain the ability to add or replace capacity and must be considered in policy and permitting timelines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide empirical supply-chain data (lead times, component shortages) and recommend mitigation (inventory strategies, prioritization of critical materials, domestic production incentives) so regulatory timelines are realistic and actionable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strengthen cybersecurity, physical-security, winter-preparedness, and supply-chain reliability
rubrics_metrics.description: FERC and NERC actions to strengthen reliability include requiring NERC to develop enhanced cybersecurity standards for internal network security protocols; directing enhancements to winter preparedness measures; approving new reliability standards to protect the electric system supply chain; and creating incentives to reward cybersecurity investments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When commenting on rules, include proposals for enhanced cybersecurity standards, supply-chain risk management, winterization requirements, and incentives for resilience investments. Cite the listed FERC/NERC measures as examples and propose how new rules should coordinate with these reliability programs.
